threads.topic: The intent to de-risk the remaining £36m LOBO book

entries.committee: Cabinet — next treasury update (mid-year to Council; no date printed in this paper)
entries.q: §4.7.5 signals more prepayment or restructure activity when the opportunity allows, following the Phoenix mutual redemption in April 2025. What is the shape of the remaining £36m — how much is one lender versus several, and is there a break-cost threshold or IRR test the paper does not print that would trigger the next tranche?
entries.why: Across the councils we have read, Merton is one of the few that has retired a LOBO by mutual agreement rather than in response to a lender call. §4.7.5 is unusually explicit about intent. If more transactions are in prospect, the timing test matters.

threads.topic: The new unrealised gain/loss reserve for the pooled property fund

entries.q: §5.1 records the decision to create an unrealised gain/loss reserve at 31 March 2026 for the first time, given the override may not be extended past 1 April 2029. Is this being sized against the £15.9m pooled property fund only, or against the whole set of pre-1 April 2024 investments the override covers?
entries.why: The 2029 cliff is a real one — an override-end reserve is a growing feature in TMSSes we have read this year, and the size ratio (reserve / covered investment) is the interesting number.

summary.text:
Merton's annual review reads like a set of pages a treasurer wrote calmly. General Fund CFR closes 2025/26 at £118m, external borrowing at £38m, internal borrowing at £54m — the identity CFR minus external minus other long-term liabilities ties to the internal-borrowing line to the pound. The council is a net investor of £157.3m (§4.4), one of the least indebted councils in London, and §4.6.4 says so plainly: 'as at 31 December 2025, Merton ranked third lowest in the long-term debt category across both inner and outer London boroughs. The average level of borrowing per council is £639 million, compared with Merton's debt level of only £38 million.'

The whole £38m is legacy: £36m of LOBO at 6.09% with 35 years weighted average maturity, plus £2m of a fixed-term market loan at 8.37% with two years to run. There is no PWLB — the council has taken no new borrowing since 2007. The liability benchmark is negative throughout the forecast and no new borrowing is planned before 2028.

The concrete piece of activity in the year, and the one worth reading twice, is §4.7.1: 'successfully repaid a £4m LOBO loan in April 2025 using a favourable settlement option. This has resulted in an annual saving of £239k in interest expenses and a total saving of approximately £2.4m over the remaining maturity period of the loan.' The §4.7.4 table names it — Phoenix, £4m, 5.99%, final maturity 04/10/2035, 'Redeemed early through mutual agreement'. Across every other treasury paper we have read this year with LOBOs on the book, we have logged Dexia calls at Kent and Tameside, refused calls at Harrow, Staffordshire and Wolverhampton, upcoming calls at Newport, KBC options going floating at Bath and NE Somerset, and £81m of open options at Newcastle. Merton is on the OPPOSITE side of that pattern — no lender call, a mutually agreed exit. §4.7.5 signals intent to do more of the same when the opportunity allows.

Investments are Arlingclose-shaped: £79.8m in government bonds at 4.22%, £50m of LA deposits at 4.75% (a zero-to-fifty step in the year), £25m of banks at 4.11%, £24.6m of MMFs at 3.82%, and £15.9m of pooled property fund. Investment income beat budget by £0.9m (£9.8m actual against £8.9m). CHAS receipts from 2023 still account for £131.3m of the £195.3m pool. Under §5.1 the council has decided to hold an unrealised gain/loss reserve at 31 March 2026 for the first time, on the basis that the statutory override may not be extended past 1 April 2029.

Every prudential indicator complies. The paper is well laid out, cleanly written, and short. A handful of typos and small unreconciled totals (£198.3m in §4.8.2 narrative vs £195.3m in Table 4; £227.9m vs £227.2m opening totals) sit inside the paper but are not worth raising.

officer.body:
Hi Nemashe,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your annual review that went to Cabinet on 13 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is short, cleanly written and reads like a set of pages someone wrote calmly, which is not universal.

Scope first. Merton has no PWLB debt and our file shows the same — we hold nothing under any Merton name — so nothing below is a claim about your loan book against a Table 3, because there isn't one to reconcile against. The whole £38m sits outside a PWLB file, being £36m of LOBO plus the £2m fixed-term market loan.

The line that caught our eye is your §4.7.1: the Phoenix £4m repaid in April 2025 through mutual agreement, £239k a year and about £2.4m over the remaining life. Across every other TMSS we've read this year that carries LOBOs, we've logged something else entirely — Dexia calls at two councils, refused calls at three more, three upcoming calls at Newport, KBC options going floating at Bath and NE Somerset, and £81m of live options at Newcastle. Merton is the exception in that pattern: no lender call, a mutually agreed exit. §4.7.5 signals more of the same when the opportunity allows, and given the £36m remaining is quiescent for the next twelve months (§4.7.5 again), that's a live piece of intent rather than a paragraph of boilerplate.

Something concrete we can offer against it: your loan-analysis page on the platform prices every LOBO in the sector against today's DMO repayment curve, so once you have a counterparty in view you can see the shape of what a mutually agreed exit might look like in current-day terms before anyone picks up the phone. Standard caveats and we mean them: we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and any figure we show is indicative only. It's at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On the investment side, §5.1 caught our attention too. You've decided to hold an unrealised gain/loss reserve at 31 March 2026 for the first time, on the basis that the pooled-investment statutory override may not be extended past 1 April 2029. That's early. Most councils we've read have kept the reserve conversation off the balance sheet until 2028. If the pooled property fund at £15.9m (§4.8.9) is the covered position, the reserve size is a decision worth having in front of it before the override cliff arrives — and doing it now, three and a half years ahead, gives you the optionality most others won't have.

And context that isn't in your paper because it can't be: sector borrowing in July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. Ten-year certainty closed at 5.83% on Thursday (notice 314/26 PM); 25-year at 6.46%; 50-year at 6.27%. Not directly relevant to Merton this year given the 2028 first-borrowing date, but useful reference for the mid-year update. The full breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit Merton. LOBO loans (legacy) is written for exactly your position. Debt restructuring covers what the Phoenix transaction looked like from both sides. IFRS 9 pooled investments and the statutory override is the direct read for the §5.1 reserve decision. And Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given the Arlingclose chart on page 232 shows the benchmark diverging further below zero out to 2075. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
